short.en: A different view, the same structure

t.en: A different problem. When you climb stairs, each stride can go up 1 step or 2 steps. How many different ways are there to reach step n?
Treat each step as a cell and lay them out in a row. Step 0 is the ground.
The last stride onto step 5 is either 1 step up from step 4, or 2 steps up from step 3.

This time the robot walks along the row of steps, starting from the ground (step 0) and moving right one step at a time. But the step 2 below is two cells away, out of reach of a 3×3 view. So for this level your robot is upgraded to Farsight, with a 5×5 view. In the This cell panel, “is ground” is “yes” only on step 0.
Build a board. With Boxy you found that parts care about structure, not names. Have you seen the structure of stair climbing somewhere before?

goal.en: Each stride goes up 1 or 2 steps, starting from the ground (step 0). Work out how many ways there are to reach steps 4, 6 and 9.

how.en: The robot goes up from step 0 (the ground), one step at a time. Standing on the ground counts as 1 way. In the view, one cell left of the red frame is 1 step down, and two cells left is 2 steps down.

body.en: If you used the Route Counter, you’ll have noticed: it has no idea it is counting stairs, and yet it got them right.

City crossings and staircases look completely unrelated, but they share a structure: every cell’s answer comes from a few earlier cells, plus a starting point. Learning to see that structure is the most important step in learning dynamic programming.

note.en: Climbing stairs: step i = step i − 1 + step i − 2, with the ground counting as 1 way.

hints.en: The last stride might be 1 step or 2 steps: add up “1 step down” and “2 steps down”.
The ground counts as 1 way: wire “is ground” into a Pass gate’s condition port and a Constant 1 into its number port.
You can also use the Route Counter directly: 1 step down into its “up”, 2 steps down into “left”, and is ground into “start”.
